title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: At five in the morning it was still completely dark. The troops at the center, the reserves, and Bagration's right flank had not yet moved, but on the left flank the columns of infantry, cavalry, and artillery — the ones designated to descend the heights first, attack the French right flank, and drive it into the Bohemian mountains according to plan — were already up and stirring. The smoke from campfires, into which the soldiers were tossing everything they couldn't carry, stung their eyes. It was cold and dark. Officers were hurriedly drinking tea and eating breakfast; soldiers were munching on biscuits and stamping their feet to keep warm, gathered around the fires and feeding the flames with the remains of sheds, chairs, tables, wheels, barrels, and anything else they didn't need or couldn't take. Austrian column guides moved back and forth among the Russian troops, serving as harbingers of the advance. As soon as an Austrian officer appeared near a commanding officer's quarters, the regiment began to move: soldiers ran from the fires, shoved their pipes into their boots, stuffed their bags into carts, grabbed their muskets, and fell into rank. Officers buttoned their coats, buckled on their swords and pouches, and walked along the ranks shouting orders. The wagon drivers and orderlies harnessed the horses and loaded the carts. The adjutants, battalion commanders, and regimental commanders mounted up, crossed themselves, gave last instructions to the baggage handlers staying behind, and the monotonous thud of thousands of marching feet echoed into the darkness. The column moved forward without knowing where it was headed, unable — because of the dense crowds around them, the smoke, and the thickening fog — to see either the place they were leaving or the place they were going.

A soldier on the march is hemmed in and carried along by his regiment just as a sailor is by his ship. No matter how far he walks, no matter what strange, unknown, or dangerous places he reaches, the soldier is always surrounded by the same familiar things — the same comrades, the same formation, the same Sergeant Major Ivan Mitrich, the same company dog Jack, the same commanding officers — just as a sailor always sees the same decks, masts, and rigging. A sailor rarely cares about the latitude his ship is crossing, but on the day of battle — who knows how or from where — a solemn, grave note sounds through the moral atmosphere of an army, one that everyone can feel. It awakens an unusual curiosity in the men. On battle day, soldiers strain to look beyond the concerns of their own regiment; they listen hard, look around eagerly, and press each other for news of what's happening.

The fog had grown so thick that even as dawn approached, they couldn't see ten paces ahead. Bushes looked like enormous trees, and flat ground appeared to be cliffs and slopes. Anywhere, on any side, an enemy invisible at ten paces might appear. But the columns marched on and on through the same fog, going downhill and uphill, past gardens and fences, across unfamiliar terrain, and nowhere did they encounter the enemy. On the contrary, the soldiers gradually became aware that in front, behind, and on every side, other Russian columns were moving in the same direction. Every soldier felt reassured to know that wherever he was headed, many more of his own were going there too.
"Look — the Kursk regiment's gone past too," voices said in the ranks.
"It's amazing how many of our troops are here, lads! Last night I looked at the campfires — there was no end to them. Like Moscow!"

Although none of the column commanders rode along the ranks or spoke to the men (the commanders, as we saw at the council of war, were in a bad mood and unhappy with the whole affair, so they simply followed orders without trying to boost morale), the troops marched cheerfully, as they always do when heading into action, especially an attack. But after about an hour of marching through the dense fog, most of the men had to stop, and an uncomfortable sense that something had gone wrong began spreading through the ranks. It's very hard to explain how such an awareness spreads, but it does — surely, imperceptibly, and unstoppably, the way water seeps into a creek bed. If the Russian army had been fighting alone without allies, it might have taken much longer for this sense of mismanagement to become a general conviction. But since there were allies, the disorder was naturally blamed on the stupid Germans, and everyone became convinced that a dangerous mix-up had been caused by the sausage-eaters.
"Why have we stopped? Is the way blocked? Or have we already run into the French?"
"No, you can't hear them. They'd be shooting if we had."
"They were in such a rush to get us started, and now here we stand in the middle of a field for no reason. It's all those damned Germans and their bungling! Stupid idiots!"
"I'd have sent them out in front, but no — they're all crowded up behind us. And now we're standing here hungry."
"Any idea when we'll get clear? They say the cavalry is blocking the way," said an officer.
"Ah, those damned Germans! Don't even know their own country!" said another.
"What division are you?" shouted an adjutant, riding up.
"The Eighteenth."
"Then what are you doing here? You should have moved on long ago — now you won't get there before evening."
"What idiotic orders! They don't even know what they're doing themselves!" said the officer, and rode off.
Then a general rode past, shouting something angrily in a language that wasn't Russian.
"Tafa-lafa! No one can understand a word he's saying," said a soldier, imitating the general who had ridden away. "I'd shoot every one of them, the bastards!"
"We were ordered to be in position by nine, and we haven't even gotten halfway. Fine orders!" This complaint was being repeated all around.
And the energy with which the troops had set out began turning to frustration and anger at the stupid arrangements and at the Germans.

The cause of the confusion was this: while the Austrian cavalry was moving toward the left flank, the high command realized the center was too far separated from the right flank, and all the cavalry was ordered to turn back to the right. Several thousand horsemen had to cross in front of the infantry, which had no choice but to wait.

At the head of the column, an argument broke out between an Austrian guide and a Russian general. The general shouted that the cavalry must be halted; the Austrian protested that it wasn't his fault — the blame lay with the higher command. Meanwhile the troops stood around, growing listless and disheartened. After an hour's delay they finally moved forward again, descending the hill. The fog that was lifting on the heights was even thicker in the valley below. Up ahead in the fog, a shot rang out, then another — first at irregular intervals, trata... tat — then faster and more steadily, and the fighting at the Goldbach Stream began.

Having stumbled on the enemy unexpectedly down by the stream in the fog, hearing no words of encouragement from their commanders, with the sense of being late spreading through the ranks, and above all unable to see anything in front or around them in the dense mist, the Russians exchanged shots with the enemy halfheartedly, advancing and then halting, receiving no clear orders from officers or adjutants who were wandering around the fog in unfamiliar terrain, unable to find their own units. This was how the fighting began for the first, second, and third columns, which had descended into the valley. The fourth column, with Kutuzov, remained on the Pratzen Heights.

Below, where the battle was unfolding, the fog was still thick; on the higher ground it was clearing, but nothing could be seen of what was happening in front. Whether the entire enemy force was six miles away as assumed, or right there in that sea of mist, no one knew until after eight o'clock.

It was nine in the morning. The fog lay unbroken like an ocean below, but higher up at the village of Schlappanitz, where Napoleon stood surrounded by his marshals, it was completely clear. Above them stretched a pure blue sky, and the sun's enormous disk trembled like a vast, hollow, crimson buoy floating on the surface of that milky sea of mist. The whole French army — and Napoleon himself with his staff — was not on the far side of the streams and ravines of Sokolnitz and Schlappanitz, beyond which the allies had planned to take up position and begin the battle. They were on the near side, so close to the Russian forces that Napoleon could distinguish mounted men from those on foot with the naked eye. Napoleon, wearing the blue cloak from his Italian campaign, sat on his small gray Arab horse slightly ahead of his marshals. He gazed in silence at the hills that seemed to rise from the sea of mist, on which the Russian troops were moving in the distance, and he listened to the sounds of gunfire from the valley. Not a single muscle moved in his face — which in those days was still thin. His gleaming eyes were fixed intently on one point. His predictions were being confirmed. Part of the Russian force had already descended into the valley toward the ponds and lakes, and another part was leaving the Pratzen Heights — which he intended to attack and considered the key to the whole position. Through the mist he could see that in a hollow between two hills near the village of Pratzen, the Russian columns, their bayonets glinting, were streaming continuously in one direction toward the valley and disappearing into the fog one after another. From the intelligence he'd received the night before, from the sounds of wheels and footsteps his outposts had heard during the night, from the disorderly movement of the Russian columns, and from every other indication, he could see clearly that the allies believed him to be far off in front of them, that the columns moving near Pratzen were the center of the Russian army, and that this center was already weakened enough to be successfully attacked. But still he did not begin the engagement.

This was a momentous day for him — the anniversary of his coronation. Before dawn he had slept a few hours, and now refreshed, vigorous, and in high spirits, he had mounted and ridden out onto the field in that happy mood where everything seems possible and everything goes right. He sat motionless, looking at the heights visible above the mist, and his cold face wore that particular look of assured, self-satisfied happiness you see on the face of a boy who is deeply and happily in love. His marshals stood behind him, not daring to interrupt his thoughts. He looked from the Pratzen Heights to the sun emerging from the fog.

When the sun had fully risen above the mist and the fields and vapor glowed with dazzling light — as though he had been waiting for exactly this moment to begin — he drew the glove from his elegant white hand, made a signal to the marshals, and gave the order to attack. The marshals, accompanied by adjutants, galloped off in every direction, and within minutes the main body of the French army was surging rapidly toward the Pratzen Heights, which were being steadily emptied as Russian troops marched down into the valley on their left.
